stimuli.title: Reading the Enemy’s Mail: The Codebreakers of World War II
stimuli.source: Original passage written for KCE GED Prep.
stimuli.html:
[1] In the spring of 1942, a small team of U.S. Navy analysts worked in a windowless basement at Pearl Harbor, Hawaii. For months they had been studying pieces of Japanese naval radio messages, and they kept running into the same two letters: “AF.” The letters seemed to name the target of a coming attack, but no one could be sure what place they stood for. Commander Joseph Rochefort, who led the team, suspected that AF meant Midway, a tiny American base in the middle of the Pacific. Some officials in Washington believed it meant somewhere else entirely.

[2] To settle the question, the team set a trap. At its suggestion, the base at Midway sent out a radio message, deliberately left unprotected, reporting that its machine for turning seawater into drinking water had broken down. Within days, codebreakers picked up a Japanese message reporting that “AF” was short of water. The guess was confirmed. When Japanese forces arrived at Midway in early June, American aircraft carriers were waiting for them, and the battle that followed became a turning point in the war in the Pacific.

[3] Midway is one of the best-known examples of a quieter kind of warfare. During World War II, every major military sent orders by radio, and radio signals could be heard by anyone with the right equipment, including the enemy. To protect their messages, armies and navies scrambled them using codes and ciphers. The enemy, in turn, worked furiously to unscramble them. Victory on the battlefield often depended on who was winning this hidden contest.

[4] Germany placed its trust in a machine called Enigma. It looked something like a typewriter, but each time an operator pressed a key, a set of turning wheels called rotors sent an electrical signal along a different path, so the same letter could come out differently every time. The machine’s settings could be arranged in more than 150 million million million ways, and the settings changed every day. German commanders were confident that no one could read their messages.

[5] They were wrong, partly because of work that began years before the war. In the early 1930s, a young Polish mathematician named Marian Rejewski, working with his colleagues Jerzy Różycki and Henryk Zygalski, used mathematics, along with documents obtained by French intelligence, to work out the inner wiring of an Enigma machine he had never seen. The three then developed methods for reading its messages. In July 1939, weeks before Germany invaded Poland, they shared what they had learned with British and French officials.

[6] The British built on that head start at Bletchley Park, a country estate northwest of London. There, the mathematician Alan Turing and his colleague Gordon Welchman designed electromechanical machines called “bombes” that could test thousands of possible Enigma settings far faster than any person could. The bombes did not work alone, however. They needed a “crib,” a short piece of text that the codebreakers could correctly guess appeared somewhere in a message. German operators made this easier than they should have. Weather stations sent reports at the same times every day in nearly the same format, and some operators began their messages with the same phrases again and again. Each predictable habit gave the codebreakers a foothold.

[7] Codebreaking was not the work of a few lone geniuses. By 1945, nearly 10,000 people worked at Bletchley Park, and about three-quarters of them were women. They operated the bombes, sorted intercepted messages, and translated and filed what was found. In the United States, the Army and Navy recruited thousands of women, many of them schoolteachers and college students, to do similar work. All of them were sworn to secrecy, and most kept that promise for decades. The full story of Bletchley Park was not made public until the 1970s, and many of its workers died without ever telling their families what they had done.

[8] Historians still debate exactly how much the codebreakers changed the outcome of the war. Some have estimated that their work shortened the war in Europe by two years or more, though such estimates are impossible to prove. What is clear is that the contest pushed technology forward. To attack a different German cipher, British engineer Tommy Flowers built Colossus, a machine that is often counted among the world’s first electronic computers. The codebreakers set out to read the enemy’s mail; along the way, they helped open the door to the digital age.

stimuli.title: Dead Air
stimuli.source: Original fiction written for KCE GED Prep.
stimuli.html:
[1] At WKRV, the overnight shift belonged to Tessa Larkin and a computer. The computer did most of the work. It played the songs in order, ran the recorded ads, and switched to the national news at the top of every hour. Tessa’s job was to watch the meters, read the station identification twice an hour, and answer the request line, which rang perhaps four times a night.

[2] Three of those calls, on most nights, came from Walt Pruitt.

[3] Walt was eighty-one and lived alone out on Route 9, past the grain elevator. He had worked nights for forty years as a watchman at the canning plant, and he said he had never learned how to sleep in the dark. He called at 11:30 to report the temperature on his porch thermometer. He called at 1:00 to ask what the young people were listening to these days and to say that it was mostly noise. And at 2:10, every night, he called to request “Mill Creek Waltz,” a scratchy fiddle tune that the station kept in its library only because Walt kept asking for it.

[4] Tessa had learned to answer his calls with one hand while scrolling on her phone with the other. He told long stories about the plant, about the flood of 1972, about his late wife’s terrible coffee. She said “Mm-hm” in the right places. Some nights she let the phone ring four or five times before picking up, hoping he would give up. He never did.

[5] Tonight he had called at 11:30 (fifty-one degrees, clear) and at 1:00 (noise, all of it). At 2:10, the request line sat dark.

[6] Tessa glanced at it. She glanced at the clock. At 2:14 she put her phone face down on the console. At 2:20 she picked up the station’s landline and dialed the number that was written in marker on the wall beside the board, under the words WALT — DON’T ENCOURAGE HIM. It rang eleven times. No one answered.

[7] The rules for the overnight shift were taped beside the microphone: No live talk except IDs. No dedications. No exceptions. Tessa read them twice. Then she found “Mill Creek Waltz” in the library, dragged it to the top of the list, and switched on the microphone. Her own voice sounded thin and strange in the headphones.

[8] “This is WKRV, 2:23 in the morning,” she said. “This one goes out to Walt on Route 9. Walt, if you can hear this, call the station.”

[9] The fiddle began, thin and wavering, like a voice that has not been used in years. Tessa sat with both hands flat on the desk and watched the request line.

[10] The song was almost over when it lit up.

[11] “You played it early,” Walt said. His voice was thick. “I dozed off in my chair. Haven’t done that in — well. Then I hear my own name coming out of the kitchen radio.”

[12] Tessa noticed that her hands were shaking. “You missed your call,” she said. “I thought —” She stopped.

[13] There was a pause on the line. “You thought you’d finally get a quiet night,” Walt said, and she could hear that he was smiling.

[14] “Something like that,” she said. She pulled the station log toward her and, in the box marked Notes, wrote: 2:31. Walt called. All fine. Then she asked him to tell her about the flood of 1972, and this time she listened to the whole thing.

stimuli.title: Let Office Employees Work Remotely Full Time
stimuli.source: By Dr. Noor Haddad, labor economist. Original passage written for KCE GED Prep.
stimuli.html:
For decades, office work meant a daily commute, a cubicle, and a supervisor within sight. The pandemic proved that much of that routine was unnecessary. Companies should now allow office employees who want to work remotely full time to do so.

The strongest reason is that remote work does not hurt productivity, and it often improves it. In a two-year study at a large insurance company, researchers randomly assigned about 1,200 claims processors either to work from home or to stay in the office. Both groups handled the same kinds of claims and were measured by the same standards. The remote group processed 6 percent more claims per day, with no increase in errors. Because workers were assigned by chance, the difference cannot be explained by more motivated employees choosing to stay home.

Remote work also saves workers time and money. The average American worker spends about 27 minutes commuting each way, according to the U.S. Census Bureau. Over a typical work year of 250 days, that adds up to about 225 hours, more than five full 40-hour work weeks. Remote employees can spend those hours with their families, exercising, or simply resting, and they spend less on gas, parking, and work clothes.

Companies benefit as well. In the same insurance study, employees who worked from home were about one-third less likely to quit during the two years than those who stayed in the office. Every employee who leaves must be replaced, and replacing a worker can cost a company thousands of dollars in recruiting and training. Firms that allow remote work can also hire from anywhere, rather than only from people who live within driving distance of the office.

Critics warn that remote workers feel isolated or miss out on mentoring. Those concerns deserve to be taken seriously, but they are problems to solve, not reasons to force everyone back to a desk. Regular video meetings, occasional in-person gatherings, and assigned mentors can keep teams connected and help new employees learn.

Office workers have shown that they can do their jobs well from home. Companies that insist otherwise will lose talented people to employers that trust them.

stimuli.title: Full-Time Remote Work Shortchanges Workers and Companies
stimuli.source: By Gary Lindqvist, regional operations manager. Original passage written for KCE GED Prep.
stimuli.html:
I have managed office teams for nineteen years, and I can tell you what happens when people stop coming in: something important is lost. Companies should not allow office employees to work remotely full time.

Anyone who has worked in an office knows that some of the best ideas come from unplanned conversations. A question asked at the coffee maker or a problem overheard in the hallway can lead to a solution no one would have found alone. Those moments simply do not happen on a scheduled video call.

Full-time remote work is especially hard on young employees. When new workers sit near experienced colleagues, they learn by watching and by asking quick questions. In one study of software engineers at a large technology company, newer engineers who sat on the same floor as their teammates received about 20 percent more written feedback on their work than newer engineers whose teammates worked in other buildings. Take away the shared office entirely, and beginners will lose even more of that informal coaching.

Managers have noticed the difference, too. In a survey my company conducted of 150 of its supervisors, nearly 70 percent said they believed their remote employees were less productive than those in the office. These are the people who watch the work every day, and their judgment should count.

Finally, remote work weakens loyalty. When employees never meet their coworkers in person, a job becomes just a paycheck and a laptop. It is no surprise that so many people now change jobs every year or two. The office was never just a place to work; it was the place where a company’s culture lived.

Some workers may enjoy staying home in their pajamas, but a business is not a vacation. Companies that want strong teams, well-trained young employees, and lasting loyalty should bring their people back together.

stimuli.title: From Sunlight to Socket: How Solar Panels Make Electricity
stimuli.source: Original passage written for KCE GED Prep.
stimuli.html:
[1] On a clear day at noon, sunlight delivers roughly 1,000 watts of power to every square meter of ground it strikes. That is about enough to run a microwave oven on every square meter of a parking lot. For most of human history, people could use that energy only as heat and light. Today, millions of rooftops and fields are covered with flat, dark panels that turn sunlight directly into electricity, with no moving parts, no fuel, and no noise. How do they do it?

[2] The story begins in 1839, when a 19-year-old French scientist named Edmond Becquerel noticed that certain materials produced a small electric current when they were exposed to light. Scientists came to call this the photovoltaic effect, from photo, meaning “light,” and volt, a unit used in measuring electricity. For more than a century, the effect was little more than a laboratory curiosity, because the materials that showed it turned only a tiny fraction of sunlight into electricity. Then, in 1954, three researchers at Bell Laboratories in New Jersey built a solar cell from silicon that converted about 6 percent of the sunlight striking it into electricity. Newspapers announced that the energy of the sun had at last been harnessed. Four years later, a small American satellite called Vanguard 1 carried solar cells into space, where they powered its radio for years.

[3] Silicon is still the material in most solar panels today. A solar cell is a thin wafer of silicon made in two layers. The top layer is treated with a small amount of another element, usually phosphorus, which gives it extra electrons that are free to move. The bottom layer is treated with an element such as boron, which leaves it with “holes,” places where electrons are missing. Where the two layers meet, some of the extra electrons drift across to fill holes. This movement builds up an electric field at the boundary, a kind of invisible slope that pushes electrons in only one direction.

[4] Light arrives in tiny packets of energy called photons. When a photon with enough energy strikes the silicon, it knocks an electron loose from its atom. If the loose electron is near the boundary, the electric field sweeps it toward the top layer. Thin metal lines printed on the surface of the cell collect these electrons and send them out through a wire. The electrons travel through a circuit — the lights, the refrigerator, whatever is connected — and return to the bottom of the cell, where they fill holes and the cycle begins again. As long as light keeps striking the cell, the current keeps flowing.

[5] A single cell produces only about half a volt, far too little to run a household appliance. That is why cells are wired together, usually 60 or more to a panel, and panels are wired together into larger groups called arrays. The electricity that comes out is direct current (DC), which flows steadily in one direction. Homes and the power grid, however, run on alternating current (AC), which reverses direction many times each second. A box called an inverter converts the panels’ DC into AC so that it can power ordinary outlets or flow into the grid.

[6] Typical panels sold today convert only about one-fifth of the sunlight that strikes them into electricity. Some light bounces off the surface. Some photons carry too little energy to free an electron at all, while others carry more than is needed, and the extra energy is lost as heat. Heat itself is a problem: a solar cell works less efficiently as it gets hotter, so a panel may actually produce more power on a cool, bright spring day than on a scorching afternoon in July. Engineers continue to experiment with new materials and with cells stacked in layers, each designed to capture a different part of sunlight.

[7] Solar panels also have an obvious limit: they produce electricity only when light reaches them. Output drops on cloudy days and stops entirely at night. For that reason, solar power is usually paired with other sources of electricity or with batteries that store extra energy produced during the day. Still, the basic idea has hardly changed since 1954. A thin slice of treated silicon, sitting quietly in the sun, sets electrons moving, and every one of them was set in motion by light that left the sun about eight minutes earlier.

stimuli.title: Before You Add Solar: What Homeowners Should Know
stimuli.source: A consumer guide. Original passage written for KCE GED Prep.
stimuli.html:
[1] Rooftop solar panels can lower a household’s electricity bills for decades, but not every roof is a good candidate. Before signing a contract, homeowners should ask a few practical questions.

[2] Which way does the roof face? In the Northern Hemisphere, the sun travels across the southern part of the sky, so south-facing roofs collect the most sunlight over a year. East- and west-facing roofs can still work well. North-facing roofs are usually a poor choice. The table below shows approximate yearly output for the same set of panels on roofs facing different directions, compared with a south-facing roof.

Direction the roof facesApproximate yearly output (compared with south-facing)
South100%
Southeast or southwest96%
East or west82%
North64%

Figures are typical for a moderately sloped roof in the middle latitudes of the United States. Actual results vary.

[3] Is the roof shaded? A single tree branch shading part of a panel can reduce the output of that whole panel, and sometimes of the panels connected to it, because cells wired in a chain can carry only as much current as the weakest cell. Some newer systems use small devices on each panel to limit this problem. Even so, homeowners may need to trim or remove trees, which is a trade-off, since shade also helps keep a house cool in summer.

[4] How old is the roof? Solar panels typically last 25 years or more, and their output declines slowly, often by about half a percent per year. Removing and reinstalling panels in order to replace a worn-out roof can cost thousands of dollars, so if a roof will need replacing within a few years, it is usually wiser to replace it first.

[5] What happens to extra electricity? On sunny afternoons, a home’s panels may produce more power than the household is using. Depending on the local utility’s rules, that extra electricity may flow into the grid in exchange for a credit on the bill, or it may be stored in a home battery. Because these rules differ widely from place to place and can change, homeowners should ask their utility how extra power is handled before estimating their savings.

[6] Have you compared offers? Prices, equipment, and warranties vary a great deal. Getting quotes from at least three installers and comparing them carefully can save a homeowner thousands of dollars over the life of a system.

items.prompt: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the passage?
options: Germany’s Enigma machine was the most advanced cipher device of its time and was never broken during the war.
The Battle of Midway was won mainly because American aircraft carriers outnumbered the Japanese fleet.
Codebreaking in World War II was a large, hidden effort that shaped the war’s events and pushed technology forward.
Women made up most of the workforce at Bletchley Park but received little credit until recent decades.
items.explain:
The passage opens with codebreaking at Midway (paragraphs 1–2), explains the “hidden contest” over codes (paragraph 3), traces the breaking of Enigma (paragraphs 4–6), describes the thousands of workers involved (paragraph 7), and ends with the codebreakers’ effect on the war and on computing (paragraph 8). Only the third choice covers all of this.

The first choice contradicts paragraph 5 (“They were wrong”). The passage never compares fleet sizes at Midway. The women of Bletchley Park are one important detail in paragraph 7, not the main idea of the whole passage.

items.prompt: Why does the author begin the passage with the story of the “AF” message (paragraphs 1–2)?
options: to draw readers in with a specific, dramatic example of codebreaking changing the course of a battle
to argue that American codebreakers were more skilled than British codebreakers
to explain how the Enigma machine scrambled German messages
to show that officials in Washington usually ignored the advice of codebreakers
items.explain:
The Midway story is a vivid, concrete case: a clever trap confirmed a guess, and the result was “a turning point in the war in the Pacific.” Paragraph 3 then widens the view: “Midway is one of the best-known examples of a quieter kind of warfare.” The story hooks the reader before the author explains the larger topic.

The passage never ranks American codebreakers against British ones, and Enigma is not discussed until paragraph 4. Only “some officials” disagreed once; the passage does not say officials “usually” ignored codebreakers.

items.prompt: Paragraph 6 is shown below. Click the sentence that gives specific examples of German habits that helped the codebreakers.
spans: The British built on that head start at Bletchley Park, a country estate northwest of London.

There, the mathematician Alan Turing and his colleague Gordon Welchman designed electromechanical machines called “bombes” that could test thousands of possible Enigma settings far faster than any person could.
The bombes did not work alone, however.
They needed a “crib,” a short piece of text that the codebreakers could correctly guess appeared somewhere in a message.
German operators made this easier than they should have.
Weather stations sent reports at the same times every day in nearly the same format, and some operators began their messages with the same phrases again and again.
Each predictable habit gave the codebreakers a foothold.
items.explain:
The sixth sentence names two concrete habits: weather reports sent at the same times “in nearly the same format” and messages that began “with the same phrases again and again.” These predictable texts made good cribs.

The sentence “German operators made this easier than they should have” makes a general claim but gives no examples, and the last sentence states the result of the habits rather than describing them.

items.prompt: Based on paragraph 2, why did the codebreakers want Midway’s message about the broken water machine to be sent without protection?
options: They wanted the American forces on Midway to know that their drinking water was unsafe.
They expected Japanese listeners to read it and repeat the news in their own coded messages, revealing what “AF” meant.
They had no secure way to communicate with the base at Midway.
They hoped the message would convince Japan to cancel its attack.
items.explain:
The message was a “trap.” Because it was “deliberately left unprotected,” the Japanese could easily read it. When a Japanese message then reported that “AF” was short of water, the codebreakers knew AF meant Midway: “The guess was confirmed.”

The water machine had not really broken, so there was no unsafe water to warn about. Nothing suggests the codebreakers lacked secure communication or wanted Japan to cancel the attack; in fact, American carriers were “waiting” for the attack.

items.prompt: As it is used in paragraph 6, the word foothold most nearly means
options: a physical weakness in a machine
a reason to stop working
a place to hide
a starting point from which to make progress
items.explain:
A foothold is literally a secure place to put your foot when climbing. In paragraph 6, each predictable German habit supplied a crib, which gave the codebreakers a starting point for testing Enigma settings and moving forward with the work.

The habits belonged to operators, not machines, and they helped the codebreakers continue, not stop or hide.

items.prompt: The passage about the codebreakers does not tell its story in time order. Using the dates it gives, arrange these four events from earliest to latest by dragging each one into the correct position.
choices: The Battle of Midway is fought.
Polish mathematicians work out the inner wiring of the Enigma machine.
The full story of Bletchley Park is made public.
Polish experts share their findings with British and French officials.
items.explain:
(1) Rejewski and his colleagues worked out Enigma’s wiring “in the early 1930s” (paragraph 5). (2) They shared their findings “in July 1939” (paragraph 5). (3) The Battle of Midway took place in June 1942 (paragraphs 1–2). (4) Bletchley Park’s story “was not made public until the 1970s” (paragraph 7).

Notice that the passage does not present events in time order: it starts in 1942 and then goes back to the 1930s, so you must use the dates rather than the paragraph order.

items.prompt: In paragraph 7, the author states that codebreaking “was not the work of a few lone geniuses.” Which details from the passage best support this claim? Select two answers.
options: Nearly 10,000 people worked at Bletchley Park by 1945.
Alan Turing and Gordon Welchman designed the bombes.
The U.S. Army and Navy recruited thousands of women to do codebreaking work.
Enigma’s settings changed every day.
Tommy Flowers built Colossus to attack a different German cipher.
Most codebreakers kept their work secret for decades.
items.explain:
The claim is that codebreaking took large numbers of people. The nearly 10,000 workers at Bletchley Park and the thousands of women recruited in the United States both show the size of the effort.

The details about Turing, Welchman, and Flowers spotlight individual inventors, which does not show a large workforce. Enigma’s daily changes and the workers’ long secrecy are true but do not show how many people did the work.

items.prompt: Which statement best describes the author’s view of historians’ estimates about how much the codebreakers shortened the war (paragraph 8)?
options: The author rejects the estimates because the codebreakers’ work was kept secret.
The author believes the estimates are too low.
The author treats the estimates as reasonable but impossible to confirm.
The author thinks the estimates matter more than the codebreakers’ effect on technology.
items.explain:
The author reports the estimates without disputing them (“Some have estimated…”) but adds a caution: “such estimates are impossible to prove.” The author then turns to what “is clear,” the push to technology. This is a careful, balanced view: the estimates are possible, but they cannot be confirmed.

The author does not reject the estimates or call them too low. The phrase “What is clear” actually gives the technology point more certainty than the estimates, which is the opposite of the last choice.

items.prompt: How does paragraph 5 relate to paragraph 4?
options: It shows that the German confidence described in paragraph 4 was mistaken by explaining how Enigma was first broken.
It gives more technical detail about how the rotors inside Enigma worked.
It describes a different cipher that Germany used in place of Enigma.
It explains why Germany changed Enigma’s settings every day.
items.explain:
Paragraph 4 ends, “German commanders were confident that no one could read their messages.” Paragraph 5 begins, “They were wrong,” and then explains how Polish mathematicians worked out Enigma’s wiring and methods for reading its messages. Paragraph 5 contrasts with and corrects paragraph 4.

Paragraph 5 does not describe the rotors, another cipher (the “different German cipher” attacked by Colossus is mentioned only in paragraph 8), or the reason for daily setting changes.

items.prompt: Why does Tessa put her phone face down at 2:14 (paragraph 6)?
options: She has decided to rest until the next station identification.
She is growing worried because Walt has not called, and she is giving the situation her full attention.
She wants to hide her phone in case her supervisor arrives.
She is annoyed that the request line has been ringing too often.
items.explain:
Walt calls “at 2:10, every night,” but tonight “the request line sat dark.” Tessa keeps glancing at the line and the clock, and a few minutes later she phones Walt herself. Putting down the phone she usually scrolls on (paragraph 4) shows that her attention has shifted to Walt.

Nothing in the story mentions a supervisor or resting, and the line is silent, not ringing too often.

items.prompt: In paragraph 9, the narrator says the fiddle music began “thin and wavering, like a voice that has not been used in years.” This comparison mainly suggests that
options: the station’s equipment is broken and needs to be replaced
Tessa dislikes old-fashioned music
the song is too quiet for listeners to hear
the song, like Walt himself, seems old and fragile, adding to the tension of the moment
items.explain:
The simile compares the music to an old, unused voice. This fits Walt, an eighty-one-year-old man who lives alone, and it comes at the moment when Tessa does not know whether he is all right. The fragile sound mirrors her fear for him.

The comparison describes the sound of an old recording, not broken equipment or volume, and nothing in this paragraph shows Tessa’s opinion of the music.

items.prompt: How does Tessa’s attitude toward Walt change over the course of the story?
options: She moves from treating his calls as a chore to genuinely caring about him and listening to him.
She moves from admiring him to feeling embarrassed by his stories.
She moves from fearing him to pitying him.
She stays annoyed by him but follows the station’s rules more carefully.
items.explain:
Early on, Tessa answers Walt “with one hand while scrolling on her phone” and sometimes lets the phone ring, “hoping he would give up” (paragraph 4). By the end, she has broken the rules to reach him, and “this time she listened to the whole thing” (paragraph 14).

She never admires or fears him at the start, and she does not follow the rules more carefully; she breaks them by making a live dedication.

items.prompt: Paragraph 6 is shown below. Click the sentence that first shows Tessa taking action, beyond what her job requires, to check on Walt.
spans: At 2:14 she put her phone face down on the console.
At 2:20 she picked up the station’s landline and dialed the number that was written in marker on the wall beside the board, under the words WALT — DON’T ENCOURAGE HIM.
items.explain:
Tessa’s job is only to answer the request line. Calling Walt herself at 2:20 is the first time she reaches out to check on him.

Glancing at the line and the clock and putting the phone down show growing worry but are not actions toward Walt. The last two sentences describe the result of her call.

items.prompt: Which statement best expresses a theme of the story?
options: Rules exist for good reasons and should never be broken.
Machines have made human workers unnecessary.
Small, ordinary connections between people can matter more than we realize until they seem to be lost.
Older people should not live alone in the country.
items.explain:
Tessa treats Walt’s nightly calls as a nuisance until the one night he does not call. Her worry, her decision to break the rules, and her new willingness to listen show that the routine connection mattered to her more than she knew.

The story favors Tessa’s choice to break a rule, so the first choice is the opposite of its message. The computer does routine work, but the story centers on a human connection. Walt’s living situation is a detail, not a lesson the story teaches.

items.prompt: Which details best show that Walt’s calls to the station had been going on for a long time? Select two answers.
options: The station kept “Mill Creek Waltz” in its library only because Walt kept asking for it.
Walt’s phone number was written in marker on the wall beside the board.
Walt said the young people’s music was mostly noise.
The overnight rules were taped beside the microphone.
The computer switched to the national news at the top of every hour.
Walt lived past the grain elevator on Route 9.
items.explain:
A song kept in the library “only because Walt kept asking for it” shows repeated requests over time. A phone number written on the wall, with a warning from staff, shows that Walt was a familiar caller well known at the station.

Walt’s opinion of new music, the posted rules, the hourly news, and Walt’s address say nothing about how long he had been calling.

items.prompt: The words written above Walt’s phone number, “WALT — DON’T ENCOURAGE HIM,” suggest that
options: Walt had once threatened the station’s staff
other people at the station had also found Walt’s frequent calls tiresome
Tessa wrote the note to remind herself to call Walt
the station manager was worried about Walt’s health
items.explain:
“Don’t encourage him” means “don’t give him a reason to call more or talk longer.” Someone at the station wrote it as a warning, which shows that Tessa was not the only one who found his many calls tiresome.

There is no sign of a threat, and the note discourages contact rather than reminding anyone to call or showing concern for his health.

items.prompt: In paragraph 5, the author includes “(fifty-one degrees, clear)” and “(noise, all of it)” mainly to
options: show that Tessa writes down everything Walt says
suggest that Walt’s health is getting worse
explain why Tessa dislikes Walt’s calls
show how predictable Walt’s calls are, which makes the silence at 2:10 stand out
items.explain:
Paragraph 3 explained what Walt says in each call. Because his calls are so predictable, the author can sum up the 11:30 and 1:00 calls in a few words in parentheses. That quick, routine rhythm sets up the surprise of the next sentence: “At 2:10, the request line sat dark.”

Tessa does not write anything down until the end, the summaries show Walt acting normally rather than declining, and the parentheses do not explain her feelings.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the newsletter. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“The broken dryers have had a serious {{0}} on residents, especially families with young children.”

options: affect
effect
effects
affected

items.explain:
After the article “a” and the adjective “serious,” the sentence needs a singular noun. Effect is the noun meaning “a result.”

“Affect” is usually a verb (“to influence”), “affected” is a verb form, and “effects” is plural, which does not match “a.”

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the newsletter. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“The installation crew from Dalton Appliance, along with two members of the building staff, {{0}} expected to finish the work by November 6.”

options: are
were
is
have been

items.explain:
The subject is crew, which is singular. The phrase set off by commas, “along with two members of the building staff,” does not make the subject plural. A singular subject needs is.

“Are,” “were,” and “have been” are plural forms that wrongly agree with “members.”

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the newsletter. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“The association has updated {{0}} bylaws so that officers will now serve two-year terms instead of one.”

options: its
it’s
its’
there

items.explain:
The bylaws belong to the association, so the sentence needs the possessive pronoun its, which never takes an apostrophe.

“It’s” means “it is,” “its’” is not a word, and “there” refers to a place.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the newsletter. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“Elections for president, secretary, and treasurer will take place at our next general meeting, which is {{0}}.”

options: on tuesday, November 10, at the Eastside Public Library
on Tuesday, november 10, at the Eastside Public Library
on Tuesday, November 10, at the eastside public library
on Tuesday, November 10, at the Eastside Public Library

items.explain:
Days of the week (Tuesday), months (November), and the full name of a specific place (Eastside Public Library) are proper nouns and must be capitalized.

Each other option leaves one of these proper nouns in lowercase.

items.prompt:
Read these sentences from the newsletter. Choose the option that correctly completes them.

“Last winter, we collected 140 coats for families in our complex and the surrounding neighborhood. {{0}}, many children still waited at the bus stop in thin jackets.”

options: Therefore
For example
Even so
Likewise

items.explain:
The second sentence contrasts with the first: the drive collected many coats, but children still went without. Even so signals that contrast.

“Therefore” signals a result (the coats did not cause children to go cold), “For example” introduces an example, and “Likewise” signals a similarity.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the newsletter. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“The coat drive begins November {{0}} can be left in the blue bin in either lobby.”

options: 1, donations
1; donations
1 donations
1, however, donations

items.explain:
“The coat drive begins November 1” and “donations can be left in the blue bin” are both complete sentences. A semicolon correctly joins two closely related independent clauses.

A comma alone creates a comma splice, no punctuation creates a run-on, and “however” with commas on both sides is still a comma splice (and “however” wrongly signals a contrast).

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the newsletter. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“Volunteers will sort the coats by size, {{0}}, and deliver them to the Eastside Family Center.”

options: folding them into labeled bags
fold them into labeled bags
to fold them into labeled bags
they will fold them into labeled bags

items.explain:
The sentence lists three actions after “will”: sort, ___, and deliver. To keep the list parallel, the middle item must use the same base verb form: fold.

“Folding,” “to fold,” and “they will fold” each break the pattern of the series.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the newsletter. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“If you have questions about any of these items, please contact our secretary, Ms. Ortiz, or {{0}}.”

options: I
myself
me
mine

items.explain:
The pronoun is an object of the verb “contact,” so it needs the object form me. Test it alone: “please contact me.”

“I” is a subject pronoun, “myself” is used only when the subject of the sentence is also “I,” and “mine” is possessive.

essay.prompt:
The articles present arguments from a supporter and a critic of allowing office employees to work remotely full time.

In your response, analyze both positions presented in the articles to determine which one is best supported. Use relevant and specific evidence from both articles to support your response.

Type your response in the box. This task may require approximately 45 minutes to complete.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the incident report. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“At approximately 2:15 p.m., room attendant Dana Reyes {{0}} on a puddle of water in the third-floor hallway and fell, landing on her left wrist.”

options: slips
has slipped
slipped
will slip

items.explain:
The report describes a completed event at a specific past time (“At approximately 2:15 p.m.”), and the second verb in the sentence, “fell,” is in the simple past. The verb must match: slipped.

“Slips” is present tense, “has slipped” does not go with a specific past time, and “will slip” is future.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the incident report. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“Pushing her supply cart ahead of her, {{0}} until it was too late.”

options: the puddle was not visible to Ms. Reyes
the puddle went unnoticed
Ms. Reyes did not notice the puddle
there was no chance of seeing the puddle

items.explain:
The opening phrase “Pushing her supply cart ahead of her” must describe the subject that comes right after the comma. The person pushing the cart is Ms. Reyes, so she must be the subject.

In the other choices, the phrase seems to describe the puddle or “there,” which creates a dangling modifier: a puddle cannot push a cart.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the incident report. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“Staff on the floor said {{0}} had been no warning sign in the area.”

options: they’re
their
there

items.explain:
The sentence needs the word that introduces the existence of something: “there had been no warning sign.” That is there.

“They’re” means “they are,” and “their” shows ownership; neither fits.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the incident report. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“Ms. Reyes was taken to the employee health {{0}} a nurse wrapped her wrist and recommended an X-ray.”

options: office. Where
office, where
office where,
office; where

items.explain:
“Where a nurse wrapped her wrist…” is a dependent clause that adds information about the office. It should be joined to the main clause with a comma: office, where.

Starting a new sentence with “Where” creates a fragment. A semicolon must join two independent clauses, and a comma after “where” splits the clause in the wrong place.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the incident report. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“Two {{0}} written statements are attached to this report.”

options: employees
employee’s
employees’
employees’s

items.explain:
The statements belong to two employees, so the word must be plural and possessive. For a plural noun ending in s, add only an apostrophe: employees’.

“Employees” has no apostrophe to show ownership, “employee’s” refers to only one employee, and “employees’s” is never correct.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the incident report. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“A maintenance worker found that a {{0}} fitting on the water line behind the machine had been dripping for several hours.”

options: loose
lose
losing
lost

items.explain:
The sentence needs an adjective meaning “not tight”: loose.

“Lose” and “losing” are verb forms meaning to misplace or fail to win, and a “lost” fitting would be missing, which cannot drip.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the incident report. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“Until now, the ice machines on each floor {{0}} been inspected once a month.”

options: is
having
has
have

items.explain:
The subject is machines, which is plural (“on each floor” is a prepositional phrase that does not change the subject). With “been inspected,” the plural helping verb is have.

“Has” is singular and wrongly agrees with “floor.” “Is been” is not a correct verb form, and “having” cannot serve as the main verb of a sentence.

items.prompt:
Read these sentences from the incident report. Choose the option that correctly completes them.

“Maintenance replaced the fitting the same afternoon. {{0}}, all ice machines will now be checked once a week, and every housekeeping cart will carry a folding wet-floor sign.”

options: Nevertheless
For instance
As a result
Otherwise

items.explain:
The new weekly checks and wet-floor signs are changes made because of the incident. As a result shows that cause-and-effect relationship.

“Nevertheless” signals contrast, “For instance” introduces an example, and “Otherwise” signals an alternative; none of these fits.

items.prompt: Which sentence most accurately sums up what the author of “From Sunlight to Socket” wants readers to understand overall?
options: Solar cells turn sunlight directly into electricity by using layers of treated silicon to set electrons moving, a process that has improved over time but still has limits.
Solar power will soon replace all other sources of electricity because sunlight is free.
Edmond Becquerel’s discovery in 1839 quickly led to practical solar panels.
Solar panels are most useful in space, where clouds never block the sunlight.
items.explain:
Most of the passage explains how a silicon cell frees and moves electrons (paragraphs 3–5). It also traces the technology’s history (paragraph 2) and describes its limits: efficiency (paragraph 6) and darkness (paragraph 7). The first choice covers all of these.

The passage says solar is “usually paired with other sources,” not that it will replace them. Becquerel’s discovery stayed “a laboratory curiosity” for over a century. Vanguard 1 is a single detail, and the passage never claims panels are most useful in space.

items.prompt: What is the main purpose of paragraph 2?
options: to argue that Bell Laboratories deserves more credit than Edmond Becquerel
to describe how silicon is treated with phosphorus and boron
to trace how the photovoltaic effect went from a laboratory discovery to a practical technology
to explain why solar panels work less efficiently in hot weather
items.explain:
Paragraph 2 moves through time: Becquerel’s 1839 discovery, more than a century as “a laboratory curiosity,” the 1954 silicon cell, and solar cells in space by 1958. It shows how the effect became useful.

The paragraph does not compare who deserves credit. Treating silicon is explained in paragraph 3, and heat is discussed in paragraph 6.

items.prompt: Based on the passage, put the steps in the order they happen as sunlight becomes electricity used in a home. Drag each step into the correct position.
choices: An inverter changes direct current into alternating current.
A photon strikes the silicon and knocks an electron loose.
Household appliances run on the electricity.
The electric field at the boundary pushes the electron toward the top layer.
Thin metal lines on the cell’s surface collect electrons and send them into a wire.
items.explain: (1) A photon knocks an electron loose (paragraph 4). (2) The electric field “sweeps it toward the top layer” (paragraph 4). (3) Metal lines “collect these electrons and send them out through a wire” (paragraph 4). (4) The panels’ DC must pass through an inverter, which converts it to AC (paragraph 5). (5) The AC then powers “ordinary outlets” and the appliances plugged into them (paragraph 5).

items.prompt: In paragraph 2, newspapers announced that the energy of the sun had “at last been harnessed.” As it is used here, harnessed most nearly means
options: measured accurately
captured and put to use
wasted
discovered by accident
items.explain:
A harness lets a person control an animal’s strength and put it to work. The 1954 silicon cell turned a useful share of sunlight into electricity for the first time, so the sun’s energy had been captured and put to use.

The photovoltaic effect had already been discovered in 1839, so “discovered by accident” does not fit “at last.” The sentence celebrates success, not waste or measurement.

items.prompt: Paragraph 6 is shown below. Click the sentence that explains why a solar panel can produce more electricity on a cool day than on a hot one, even when the sunlight is equally bright.
spans: Typical panels sold today convert only about one-fifth of the sunlight that strikes them into electricity.
Some light bounces off the surface.
Some photons carry too little energy to free an electron at all, while others carry more than is needed, and the extra energy is lost as heat.
Heat itself is a problem: a solar cell works less efficiently as it gets hotter, so a panel may actually produce more power on a cool, bright spring day than on a scorching afternoon in July.
Engineers continue to experiment with new materials and with cells stacked in layers, each designed to capture a different part of sunlight.
items.explain:
The fourth sentence states the cause directly: “a solar cell works less efficiently as it gets hotter,” and gives the example of a cool spring day versus a hot July afternoon.

The third sentence mentions heat, but it explains how energy is wasted as heat inside the cell, not why air temperature changes a panel’s output.

items.prompt: According to paragraph 5, why are many solar cells wired together in a single panel?
options: to change direct current into alternating current
to keep the cells from overheating
so that electrons can return to the bottom layer of each cell
because one cell produces only about half a volt, too little to run household appliances
items.explain:
Paragraph 5 says, “A single cell produces only about half a volt, far too little to run a household appliance. That is why cells are wired together.”

The inverter, not the wiring of cells, changes DC to AC. The passage never links wiring to overheating, and electrons return to the bottom layer through the circuit in any cell (paragraph 4).

items.prompt: In paragraph 3, the author describes the electric field as “a kind of invisible slope.” Why does the author use this comparison?
options: to help readers picture how the field pushes electrons in one direction, the way a slope makes a ball roll downhill
to show that solar panels must be installed on slanted roofs
to suggest that the electric field is dangerous to touch
to explain how photons travel from the sun to Earth
items.explain:
The field cannot be seen, so the author compares it to something familiar. Just as objects roll only one way down a slope, the field “pushes electrons in only one direction.”

The comparison is about the inside of a cell, not roof angles, safety, or how light travels.

items.prompt: Based on paragraph 7, with which statement would the author most likely agree?
options: Solar panels are not worth installing because they stop working at night.
Batteries have made other sources of electricity unnecessary.
Solar power is most dependable when it is combined with storage or other energy sources.
The design of solar cells has changed completely since 1954.
items.explain:
Paragraph 7 explains that output “stops entirely at night,” so solar power “is usually paired with other sources of electricity or with batteries.” The author sees this pairing as the practical answer to solar’s limit.

The author names the limit but does not call panels worthless. Batteries are one option, not a replacement for all other sources. The author says the basic idea “has hardly changed since 1954.”

items.prompt: According to the table in “Before You Add Solar,” if a set of panels would produce 8,000 kilowatt-hours of electricity per year on a south-facing roof, about how much would the same panels produce on an east-facing roof?
options: 1,440 kilowatt-hours
5,120 kilowatt-hours
6,560 kilowatt-hours
7,680 kilowatt-hours
items.explain:
The table shows that an east-facing roof produces about 82% as much as a south-facing roof.

8,000 × 0.82 = 6,560 kilowatt-hours.

5,120 uses the north-facing figure (8,000 × 0.64), 7,680 uses the southeast/southwest figure (8,000 × 0.96), and 1,440 is the amount lost (8,000 − 6,560), not the amount produced.

items.prompt: According to “Before You Add Solar,” which conditions reduce the amount of electricity a rooftop system produces? Select two answers.
options: a tree branch shading part of a panel
a roof that will need to be replaced in a few years
a roof that faces north
a utility that does not give credit for extra electricity
getting quotes from several installers
items.explain:
Paragraph 3 says shade on part of a panel “can reduce the output of that whole panel,” and the table in paragraph 2 shows that a north-facing roof produces only about 64% as much as a south-facing one.

An aging roof adds cost but does not lower output. A utility’s credit rules affect savings, not how much electricity the panels make. Comparing quotes affects price.

items.prompt: How does the purpose of “Before You Add Solar” differ from the purpose of “From Sunlight to Socket”?
options: “Before You Add Solar” argues against solar power, while “From Sunlight to Socket” argues for it.
“Before You Add Solar” traces the history of solar cells, while “From Sunlight to Socket” compares prices.
Each passage mainly aims to persuade readers to install panels right away.
“From Sunlight to Socket” explains how solar cells work, while “Before You Add Solar” gives practical advice to help homeowners decide whether and how to install panels.
items.explain:
“From Sunlight to Socket” explains a process: how silicon cells turn light into electricity. “Before You Add Solar” is a consumer guide organized around questions a homeowner should ask before signing a contract.

The guide does not oppose solar; it says panels “can lower a household’s electricity bills for decades.” The history is in “From Sunlight to Socket,” and prices are in the guide, so the second choice reverses them. Neither passage urges readers to buy panels right away.

items.prompt: Which idea from “From Sunlight to Socket” best helps explain why shade on one part of a panel can reduce the output of the whole panel, as described in “Before You Add Solar”?
options: Cells are wired together, usually 60 or more to a panel.
A solar cell works less efficiently as it gets hotter.
An inverter converts direct current into alternating current.
Some light bounces off the surface of a panel.
items.explain:
“Before You Add Solar” explains that “cells wired in a chain can carry only as much current as the weakest cell.” That only makes sense once you know, from “From Sunlight to Socket,” that a panel is many cells wired together. If one shaded cell is weak, it holds back the rest.

Heat, the inverter, and reflected light are real parts of solar power, but none explains why shading one small area affects a whole panel.

items.prompt: Why does the author of “Before You Add Solar” call removing trees “a trade-off” (paragraph 3)?
options: Falling branches can damage the panels.
Removing trees gives panels more sunlight but takes away shade that helps keep the house cool.
Most utilities require homeowners to remove trees before installation.
Trees can produce more energy than solar panels do.
items.explain:
A trade-off means gaining one thing by giving up another. Cutting trees removes shade from the panels, which increases output, but “shade also helps keep a house cool in summer,” so the household loses that benefit.

The passage does not mention falling branches, utility requirements about trees, or trees producing energy.
